title: Capturing the Value Chain at Home: Economics of Prosumers Using an LLM-Assisted Distributed Additive Manufacturing for Functional Products
content: Inflation, debt and erratic tariffs result in less affordable consumer goods. This makes do-it-yourself (DIY) distributed manufacturing with 3-D printing increasingly attractive. Prosumers save substantially by printing open-source designs, but customizing products has required hiring a designer or learning computer-aided design. This study evaluates a no-skill approach where a large language model (LLM) generates parametric OpenSCAD code from a reference image and a short text prompt. An economic model and decision rule are developed to determine when prosumers should 3-D print rather than buy a product. The method was tested on three functional case studies: highly-ornate shower curtain rings in PETG, a wicker weaving tool by replacing steel with PLA and anti-vibration appliance feet in flexible TPU. All three designs were customizable, printed without failure on a consumer-grade 3-D printer using default settings and performed their intended functions. The printed products saved between 84% to 97% compared to commercial products. Material costs dominated, electricity was minor, labor costs were equivalent and the LLM design cost of about $0.25 made up 7%-41% of the total. LLMs thus remove the design barrier to prosumer mass customization, but as printing costs fall AI tokens dominate, so prosumers should first search free repositories.
